decks.title: Pressure in Fluids — Part 1: Thrust, pressure and liquid columns
goals: Distinguish thrust from pressure and calculate pressure as thrust per unit area
Explain why sharp knives cut better and why heavy vehicles have broad tyres
Calculate the pressure at a depth in a liquid using p = h rho g

slides.heading: Why does a pin go in so easily?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the same push can do very different jobs depending on the area it acts on.

visual.alt: Flow showing that force and area together decide the pressure

slides.narration: Push a drawing pin with your thumb and the point goes into the board. Push the same pin the other way round and nothing happens. The force is the same. What changed is the area it acts on.

slides.heading: Thrust and pressure
slides.body_md: **Thrust** is the force acting **perpendicular** to a surface. **Pressure** is the **thrust acting on unit area**: $p = \dfrac{F}{A}$. The SI unit of pressure is the **pascal (Pa)**, which is one newton per square metre.

visual.alt: Table of thrust, area and pressure with their symbols and SI units

slides.narration: Thrust is the force pressing at right angles on a surface. Divide it by the area it presses on and you get pressure. One newton on every square metre is one pascal.

slides.heading: A brick on a sponge
slides.body_md: A brick weighing 20 N is placed on a sponge in three ways. The **thrust is the same** each time, but the **area** is different, so the pressure and the dent are different.

slides.narration: The brick always weighs the same, so the thrust never changes. Lying flat it spreads the weight over a large area and makes a shallow dent. Standing on its end it uses a small area and presses the hardest.

slides.heading: Quick check: which face presses most?
slides.body_md: Look at the three positions of the brick.

visual.alt: Table of the area and pressure for each position of the brick

slides.narration: A brick can rest on any of its faces. Which face gives the greatest pressure on the sponge?

slides.heading: Increasing and reducing pressure
slides.body_md: To get a **large pressure**, make the area **small**. To get a **small pressure**, make the area **large**.

headers: What is done to the area
rows: Edge or point has a very small area
Large pressure, so it cuts or pierces
Broad tyres of a heavy truck
Large area of contact with the road
Smaller pressure, so the tyre does not sink
Wide strap of a heavy school bag

visual.alt: Table of three everyday examples of increasing and reducing pressure by changing the area

slides.narration: A sharp knife has an edge with almost no area, so even a gentle push gives a huge pressure. A heavy truck has broad tyres to spread its weight, and a wide bag strap spreads the load on your shoulder.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a girl standing on the floor
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A girl weighs 500 N. The soles of both her feet cover 0.025 m². Find the pressure on the floor when she stands on both feet and when she lifts one foot.

**Step 1.** Thrust $F = 500$ N. On both feet: $p = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{500}{0.025} = 20000$ Pa.

**Step 2.** On one foot the area is halved, so $p = \dfrac{500}{0.0125} = 40000$ Pa.

visual.alt: Table of the area and pressure when the girl stands on two feet and on one foot

slides.narration: Her weight is the thrust on the floor. Divide it by the area of both feet to get twenty thousand pascal. Lift one foot, the area halves, and the pressure doubles to forty thousand pascal.

slides.heading: Quick check: the unit of pressure
slides.body_md: Pressure is thrust divided by area.

visual.alt: Table showing thrust in newton and area in square metre giving a unit for pressure

slides.narration: Thrust is measured in newtons and area in square metres. Which of the options is the same as one pascal?

slides.heading: Pressure inside a liquid
slides.body_md: A liquid presses on the **bottom** and on the **walls** of its container, and the pressure acts **in all directions**. At a greater depth the liquid has more weight above it, so the pressure is **greater**. A jet from a lower hole is faster.

slides.heading: Pressure of a liquid column: p = h rho g
slides.body_md: Take a column of liquid of height $h$ and base area $A$ and density $\rho$. Its weight is the thrust on the base.

rows: ρ A h g ÷ A = h ρ g

visual.alt: Table of the steps that give the pressure of a liquid column as h rho g

slides.narration: The weight of the column is density times area times height times gee. Divide by the area and the area cancels. The pressure is height times density times gee. It does not depend on the width of the column at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: pressure at the bottom of a lake
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the pressure due to the water at a depth of 8 m in a lake. ($\rho = 1000$ kg m⁻³, $g = 10$ m s⁻²)

**Step 1.** $p = h \rho g = 8 \times 1000 \times 10$.

**Step 2.** $p = 80000$ Pa.

visual.alt: Table of the data and the answer for the pressure at the bottom of a lake

slides.narration: Multiply the depth, the density and gee. Eight metres times one thousand times ten gives eighty thousand pascal. Always keep the units in kilograms per cubic metre and metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: doubling the depth
slides.body_md: Use p = h ρ g and think about what stays the same.

visual.alt: Table asking for the pressure at twice the depth

slides.narration: A diver goes down from a certain depth to twice that depth in the same lake. What happens to the pressure due to the water?

slides.heading: Pressure grows steadily with depth
slides.body_md: In water, the pressure rises by **10 000 Pa for every metre** of depth ($\rho g = 1000 \times 10$). The graph of $p$ against $h$ is a **straight line through the origin**.

visual.alt: Straight-line graph of liquid pressure against depth for water, through the origin and reaching eighty thousand pascal at eight metres
visual.caption: Pressure is proportional to depth.

slides.narration: Because density and gee do not change, the pressure grows in step with depth. The graph is a straight line through the origin. Double the depth and the pressure is doubled.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Thrust is the force perpendicular to a surface; pressure is thrust per unit area, p = F / A.
The SI unit of pressure is the pascal: 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
A small area gives a large pressure; a large area gives a small pressure.
A liquid column of height h exerts pressure p = h ρ g, and pressure increases with depth.

visual.alt: Summary table of the two pressure formulae

slides.narration: To sum up Part one. Thrust is a force at right angles to a surface. Pressure is thrust divided by area, measured in pascals. Liquids press harder at greater depth, and the pressure of a column is height times density times gee.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Convert the area to square metres before you divide: 1 cm² = 0.0001 m².
Use the weight of the body as the thrust when it rests on a surface.
Write density in kg m⁻³ and height in metres in p = h ρ g.
For reasons, always mention the area: small area, large pressure.

rows: Using area in cm² with newton and calling the answer Pa
Using the mass instead of the weight as thrust

visual.alt: Table of three common slips and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Change square centimetres to square metres before dividing. When a body rests on a surface, its weight is the thrust, not its mass. And in every explanation, mention the area.

decks.title: Pressure in Fluids — Part 2: Liquid pressure in use, and Pascal’s law
goals: State the factors on which pressure in a stationary liquid depends and those on which it does not
Explain why a dam is broader at the base and why a diver needs a special suit
State Pascal’s law and solve simple problems on force and pressure transmitted through a liquid

slides.heading: Why is a dam thicker at the bottom?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what decides the pressure in a liquid, and how a liquid passes pressure on.

nodes.label: Passed on equally by the liquid

visual.alt: Flow from depth, density and g to pressure at a point to pressure passed on equally

slides.narration: Look at a dam from the side. It is thin at the top and very thick at the bottom. The builders were using what we shall learn now about pressure in liquids.

slides.heading: What the pressure depends on
slides.body_md: The pressure at a point in a stationary liquid depends on the **depth**, the **density** of the liquid and the **acceleration due to gravity**. It does **not** depend on the shape of the vessel, the area of its base or the total amount of liquid.

rows: Total volume or weight of liquid

visual.alt: Table of the factors that decide liquid pressure and those that do not

slides.narration: Only three things matter: how deep the point is, how dense the liquid is, and the pull of gravity. A narrow tube and a wide tank of the same depth give exactly the same pressure at the bottom.

slides.heading: Three vessels, one pressure
slides.body_md: Vessels of different shape are filled to the **same height**. The pressure at the base is the **same** in all of them: here 4000 Pa.

slides.heading: Quick check: shape does not matter
slides.body_md: Think about which factor changes between the vessels.

visual.alt: Table showing that three different vessels have the same depth of liquid

slides.narration: A narrow tube, a wide tank and a funnel are filled with the same liquid to the same height. How do the pressures at their bases compare?

slides.heading: Pressure at one depth acts in all directions
slides.body_md: At a given depth, the pressure is the **same in every direction**: up, down and sideways. Points at the **same depth** in the same liquid have the **same pressure**.

rows: A bubble released at the bottom is squeezed equally on all sides
Pressure acts equally in all directions
Water in a U-tube stands at the same level in both arms
A jet from a hole near the bottom is stronger than from a hole near the top

visual.alt: Table of three observations and what each shows about liquid pressure

slides.narration: A tiny bubble deep in water is squeezed from every side by the same amount. Water in the two arms of a U-tube settles at the same level. And jets from lower holes are stronger. All three come from the same idea.

slides.heading: Dams and divers
slides.body_md: Because pressure grows with depth, the water presses much harder near the **base** of a dam. A deep-sea diver faces a large pressure on her body and needs a **strong special suit**.

rows: Dam wall broader at the base
The pressure of the water is greatest at the bottom, so the wall must be strongest there
The pressure at depth is very large and can harm the body
They live where the pressure is huge

visual.alt: Table of three situations and the reason for each in terms of pressure and depth

slides.narration: The deeper the water, the greater the pressure, so a dam needs a thick base to withstand the largest push. In the same way a diver needs a strong suit at great depths.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: force on a window under water
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A flat window of area 0.5 m² is fixed in the side of a tank at a depth of 20 m in water. Find the pressure there and the force on the window. ($\rho = 1000$ kg m⁻³, $g = 10$ m s⁻²)

**Step 1.** $p = h \rho g = 20 \times 1000 \times 10 = 200000$ Pa.

**Step 2.** $F = p \times A = 200000 \times 0.5 = 100000$ N.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the pressure and the force on the window

slides.narration: First find the pressure at that depth, which is two hundred thousand pascal. The force is pressure times area, so it is one hundred thousand newtons, about the weight of ten tonnes.

slides.heading: Liquids pass on pressure
slides.body_md: When pressure is applied to a liquid in a **closed** vessel, the liquid passes it on to **every part** of the liquid and to the walls. A sealed bottle with holes sends out equal jets all round when it is squeezed.

rows: Piston pushing on a sealed syringe of water
Squeezing a sealed plastic bag of milk
Milk is forced out of any hole with equal pressure
A hole in a squeezed ball full of water

visual.alt: Table of examples in which pressure applied to a liquid is passed on

slides.narration: Squeeze a sealed bag of milk and the pressure you apply reaches every corner. That is why milk jets out of a hole wherever it is. Liquids hardly compress, so they carry the pressure on.

slides.heading: Pascal’s law
slides.body_md: Pressure applied to an **enclosed liquid** is transmitted **equally and undiminished** to every part of the liquid and to the walls of the container. If a force $F_1$ acts on a piston of area $A_1$, the pressure $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1}$ also acts on a piston of area $A_2$, giving $F_2 = \dfrac{F_1}{A_1} \times A_2$.

sections.heading: 1. Thrust and pressure
sections.body_md:
**Thrust** is the force acting perpendicular to a surface; its SI unit is the newton. **Pressure** is the thrust acting on unit area: $p = \dfrac{F}{A}$. SI unit: **pascal (Pa)**, $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N m}^{-2}$. Convert areas first: $1\ \text{cm}^2 = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$.

- The same thrust gives a **larger pressure on a smaller area**. A brick of weight 20 N on a sponge presses most when it stands on its smallest face.
- **Large pressure (small area):** knife edge, needle, nail, axe, pointed tip of a drawing pin.
- **Small pressure (large area):** broad tyres of heavy vehicles, broad straps of a school bag, the wide feet of a camel, skis and snow shoes.
- When a body rests on a surface, its **weight** is the thrust on the surface.

sections.heading: 2. Pressure in a liquid: p = h ρ g
sections.body_md:
A liquid presses on the bottom and the walls of its container, and at a point the pressure acts equally in all directions.

**Pressure of a liquid column:** for height $h$, density $\rho$ and base area $A$, the weight of the liquid is $A h \rho g$, so the pressure is $p = \dfrac{A h \rho g}{A} = h \rho g$ (the pressure of the liquid alone; the atmosphere is not included).

**Factors:** the pressure depends on the **depth** $h$, the **density** $\rho$ of the liquid and $g$. It does **not** depend on the shape of the vessel, the area of its base or the quantity of liquid. At the same depth in the same liquid the pressure is the same.

- **Dam:** the wall is made broader at the base because the water pressure increases with depth.
- **Diver:** needs a strong special suit because of the large pressure at depth.
- A jet from a lower hole of a tall vessel is faster than from a higher hole.
- In water ($\rho = 1000$ kg m⁻³, $g = 10$ m s⁻²) the pressure rises by $10\,000$ Pa for every metre of depth. Mercury has $\rho = 13\,600$ kg m⁻³.

The pressure in a liquid that is not moving, which increases with depth.

sections.heading: 3. Transmission of pressure and Pascal’s law
sections.body_md:
Liquids are almost incompressible, so pressure applied to a liquid in a closed vessel is passed on to every part of it.

**Pascal’s law:** pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the liquid and to the walls of the container.

For a closed vessel with two pistons of areas $A_1$ and $A_2$, a force $F_1$ on the first piston gives the pressure $p = \dfrac{F_1}{A_1}$ everywhere, so the force on the second piston is $F_2 = p A_2 = F_1 \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}$.

- **Examples of transmitted pressure:** squeezing a toothpaste tube, a syringe, a sealed bag of milk with holes pricked in it.
- The **pressure** is the same on every piston; the **force** is not.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using the area in cm² in p = F / A and calling the answer Pa.
- Using the mass of a body instead of its weight as the thrust.
- Writing that liquid pressure depends on the shape or width of the vessel.
- Saying the same force acts on both pistons instead of the same pressure.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definitions (1 mark each): thrust, pressure, unit; Pascal's law in full.
- Numericals (1 to 3 marks): formula, substitution with units, answer with unit.
- Reasons (2 marks): link the area (knife, tyre) or the depth (dam, diver) to pressure.

A student places a block of weight 54 N on soft sand in three ways. Its faces measure 30 cm × 15 cm, 30 cm × 6 cm and 15 cm × 6 cm.

(a) Define thrust and pressure, and state the SI unit of pressure. [3]

(b) Calculate the pressure on the sand when the block rests on each of the three faces. [4]

(c) State, with a reason, the position in which the block sinks deepest into the sand. [2]

(d) State the thrust on the sand in each position. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Thrust** is the force acting perpendicular to a surface; **pressure** is the thrust on each unit of area; the SI unit of pressure is the **pascal** (N m⁻²).

**(b)** Thrust $= 54$ N. Areas: $450\ \text{cm}^2 = 0.045\ \text{m}^2$, $180\ \text{cm}^2 = 0.018\ \text{m}^2$, $90\ \text{cm}^2 = 0.009\ \text{m}^2$. $p = \dfrac{54}{0.045} = 1200$ Pa; $\dfrac{54}{0.018} = 3000$ Pa; $\dfrac{54}{0.009} = 6000$ Pa.

**(c)** On the **smallest face** (15 cm × 6 cm), because the same thrust acts on the smallest area and so gives the greatest pressure.

**(d)** **54 N** in every position, the weight of the block.

questions.solution_md: Definitions and Pa; 1200 Pa, 3000 Pa, 6000 Pa; smallest face; 54 N each.

A dam holds back a reservoir of water 40 m deep. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Explain why the wall of the dam is made broader at the base. [2]

(b) Find the pressure due to the water at depths of 10 m and 30 m. [3]

(c) Find the force of the water on a flat gate of area 2 m² fixed at a depth of 30 m. [2]

(d) Another reservoir behind a different dam is much wider but also 40 m deep and holds the same kind of water. Compare the pressure at the base in the two reservoirs and give the reason. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The pressure of the water **increases with depth**, so the push on the wall is greatest near the bottom. A **broad, strong base** is needed to withstand it.

**(b)** $p = h \rho g$: at 10 m, $p = 10 \times 1000 \times 10 = 100000$ Pa; at 30 m, $p = 30 \times 1000 \times 10 = 300000$ Pa.

**(c)** $F = p A = 300000 \times 2 = 600000$ N.

**(d)** The pressures at the base are **equal**. The pressure depends only on the **depth, the density of the liquid and g**, not on the width of the reservoir or the amount of water.

questions.stem_md:
A rectangular tank with a base 2.0 m by 1.5 m is filled with water to a depth of 1.2 m. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Find the pressure of the water at the base. [2]

(b) Find the force of the water on the base. [2]

(c) Find the weight of the water in the tank and compare it with your answer to (b). [3]

(d) A second vessel has the same base area but its walls lean outwards, so it is wider at the top. It is filled with water to the same depth of 1.2 m. State, with reasons, how the pressure at its base and the force on its base compare with those in the tank, and whether the force on the base equals the weight of the water in it. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $p = h \rho g = 1.2 \times 1000 \times 10 = 12000$ Pa.

**(b)** Area $= 2.0 \times 1.5 = 3.0$ m², so $F = p A = 12000 \times 3.0 = 36000$ N.

**(c)** Volume $= 3.0 \times 1.2 = 3.6$ m³; mass $= 1000 \times 3.6 = 3600$ kg; weight $= 3600 \times 10 = 36000$ N. This **equals the force on the base**, as the walls are vertical.

**(d)** The **pressure is the same**, because it depends only on depth, density and g. The **force on the base is also the same**, since pressure and base area are unchanged. But the vessel holds **more water**, so its weight is **greater than the force on the base**: the sloping walls carry the weight of the extra water.

questions.stem_md:
A diver works at a depth of 25 m in the sea. (Density of sea water 1030 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Find the pressure due to the water at this depth. [2]

(b) Find the force of the water on a flat window of area 0.02 m² on her helmet. [2]

(c) She descends to 50 m. Find the pressure there and say how it compares with that at 25 m. [3]

(d) Explain why a diver needs a special suit. [2]

(e) State the direction in which the water presses on her body. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $p = h \rho g = 25 \times 1030 \times 10 = 257500$ Pa.

**(b)** $F = p A = 257500 \times 0.02 = 5150$ N.

**(c)** $p = 50 \times 1030 \times 10 = 515000$ Pa, which is **twice** the pressure at 25 m, as the pressure is proportional to the depth.

**(d)** The pressure of the water at depth is **very large** and would harm the body; the **strong suit** protects it.

**(e)** The water presses **equally from all directions**.

questions.solution_md: 257 500 Pa; 5150 N; 515 000 Pa, double; pressure is large at depth; all directions.
